questions.question: Justify the use of cross-over electrophoresis as a confirmatory test
questions.solution_html:
• Cross-over Electrophoresis: Justified as a confirmatory test because it uses an electric field
  • to force antigens and antibodies toward each other, creating a visible precipitin line that
  • confirms species origin with high sensitivity.

questions.question: Define rouleaux formation.
questions.solution_html:
• Rouleaux Formation: The stacking of red blood cells like a "pile of coins," often occurring
  • in thick blood smears or due to certain plasma protein imbalances, which can interfere with
  • grouping.

questions.question: Demonstrate the step-by-step procedure of the Kastle–Mayer test.
questions.solution_html:
• Kastle-Mayer Procedure: 1. Rub a moist swab on the stain. 2. Add a drop of KM reagent
  • (phenolphthalein). 3. Add a drop of Hydrogen Peroxide. 4. Observe for an immediate pink
  • color.

questions.question: Explain forensic importance of polymorphic proteins.
questions.solution_html:
• Polymorphic Proteins: Proteins that exist in several different forms (variants) within a
  • population; they are forensically important because they provide a "biochemical fingerprint"
  • for individualized profiling.

questions.question: Explain the principles and procedures of presumptive and confirmatory tests for blood. Discuss the Kastle–Mayer (Phenolphthalein) test and Takayama test in detail.
questions.solution_html:
• Kastle-Mayer (Presumptive): Based on the peroxidase-like activity of hemoglobin.
  • Highly sensitive but prone to false positives from vegetable peroxidases.
  • Takayama Test (Confirmatory): Heating a bloodstain with a reagent containing
  • pyridine and glucose to form salmon-pink, pyridine-haemochromogen crystals, which are
  • viewed under a microscope.
